title: Regular-immersion geometry and intrinsic virtual dimension
statement:
Let schemes and their morphisms be as in [def-pc-scheme], with regularity [def-weil-regular-scheme], finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], smoothness [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], and closed immersions [def-weil-closed-immersion]. A regular closed immersion means one whose ideal is locally generated by a regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence]; its codimension is the locally constant length of that sequence, or equivalently the rank of its conormal module. The following hold for Noetherian schemes.

An immersion between regular schemes is regular. Regular closed immersions are preserved by flat base change and composition; their codimensions are preserved by flat base change and add under composition. A section of a separated smooth morphism of relative dimension $r$ is a regular closed immersion of codimension $r$. A scheme smooth over a regular scheme is regular.

A finite-type morphism $f:Y\to X$ between regular affine schemes admits a closed immersion $Y\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^r_X$; every such immersion is regular. For any factorization $f=pi$ with $i$ a regular closed immersion of codimension $c$ and $p$ smooth of relative dimension $r$ (locally on components), the integer $r-c$ is locally constant and satisfies, for $y\in Y$, $x=f(y)$,
$$r-c=\dim\mathcal O_{Y,y}-\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(x)}\kappa(y).$$
Dimension and transcendence degree are [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring], [def-kun-transcendence-degree], and residue fields are [def-weil-residue-field]. Thus this integer is independent of the factorization. For a quasi-finite $f$ (finite type with finite fibres), the residue extension is finite and its transcendence degree is zero. These assertions include codimension zero, relative dimension zero, and empty schemes; on the empty scheme all pointwise assertions are vacuous.

Intrinsic virtual dimension also ILO XVI Definitions 2.5.1–2.5.3; quasi-finite case XVII Lemma 2.4.3.4. Polynomial and smooth regularity are existing inputs lem-trf-polynomial-ring-regular-base and lem-weil-pbc-regular-ring-smooth-ascent; finite-type affine presentation is the polynomial presentation of a finitely generated algebra.

proof.text: For an immersion between regular Noetherian schemes, restrict the ambient scheme so that it is closed. At a source point the local ring map is a surjection $R\twoheadrightarrow R/I$ of regular local rings. The regular-local quotient theorem gives a regular system of parameters $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ of $R$ with $I=(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$. The parameter theorem says that the entire parameter system is regular, hence its initial segment is regular: its successive multiplication maps are a prefix of those for the full system, and its quotient is nonzero since all entries lie in the maximal ideal.

The stalkwise generators in Step 1 give local equations on an actual neighbourhood as follows. Choose an affine ambient neighbourhood $\operatorname{Spec}A$, with finitely generated ideal $J$ of the closed subscheme, and clear the finitely many denominators in $x_1,\ldots,x_c$ to obtain $a_1,\ldots,a_c\in J$ whose images generate $J_{\mathfrak p}$ and form a regular sequence there. Multiplication by those cleared denominators is by units at $\mathfrak p$, so regularity is unchanged. Apply the principal-neighbourhood regular-sequence lemma to the $a_i$ in the Noetherian ring $A$: the $a_i$ form a regular sequence in $A[1/g]$ for some $g\notin\mathfrak p$. Next make $J=(a_1,\ldots,a_c)$: for each of finitely many generators of $J$, its class modulo $(a_1,\ldots,a_c)$ is zero at $\mathfrak p$, so some $h_k\notin\mathfrak p$ kills it; put $h=\prod_kh_k$. The sequence stays regular in $A[1/gh]$: if $a_j\,(m/h^n)=0$ in $A[1/gh]/(a_1,\ldots,a_{j-1})$ with $m$ from $A[1/g]/(a_1,\ldots,a_{j-1})$, then $h^Na_jm=0$ for some $N$, so $h^Nm=0$ by injectivity over $A[1/g]$, i.e. $m/h^n=0$; and the final quotient $(A/J)[1/gh]$ is nonzero because $\mathfrak p$ survives. Thus the immersion is regular in the stated neighbourhood sense. For any such regular equations, the conormal-freeness theorem identifies $J/J^2$ with $(A/J)^c$ on the classes of the equations. Consequently its rank, and thus the length $c$, is independent of the equations and locally constant on the source. At a nonzero stalk, independence of free rank follows by reducing a free-module isomorphism modulo the maximal ideal.

source.place: Tag 061L, lemma-regular-sequence-in-neighbourhood; Tag 00LN, lemma-regular-quasi-regular, in degree one; divisors.tex Tag 0E9J

proof.text: For flat base change, take an affine flat ring map $A\to B$ and local equations $a_1,\ldots,a_c$ for a regular closed immersion. Put $M_j=A/(a_1,\ldots,a_j)$. Tensor every injection $M_{j-1}\xrightarrow{a_j}M_{j-1}$ with the flat $A$-module $B$. Flat tensor exactness preserves injectivity; the quotient/base-change isomorphism identifies the tensor module with $B/(a_1,\ldots,a_{j-1})B$ and the tensor map with multiplication by the image of $a_j$. At every prime of $B$ containing the image ideal the tuple is therefore regular by the weak-regular-sequence localization lemma. There is no flatness assumption on $A/(a_1,\ldots,a_c)$. Step 2 spreads these local sequences to neighbourhoods. The affine pullback is $\operatorname{Spec}(B/(a_1,\ldots,a_c)B)$ by the same quotient isomorphism, and its conormal module is free of rank $c$ by conormal freeness. This proves preservation of the regular closed immersion and of codimension.

For composition, on a local affine chart write the first ideal as $(a_1,\ldots,a_c)$ and the second ideal in its quotient as $(\bar b_1,\ldots,\bar b_e)$, with both displayed tuples regular. Lift each $\bar b_j$ to $b_j$ in the ambient ring. The composite ideal is $(a_1,\ldots,a_c,b_1,\ldots,b_e)$. In the first $c$ multiplication tests its injectivity is that of the $a$-tuple; in each subsequent test the prefix quotient is exactly the corresponding quotient by the $\bar b$-tuple, so injectivity holds there too. The final quotient is the nonzero local ring of the smallest subscheme. Hence the concatenated tuple is regular. Step 2 spreads at the point if needed, and its conormal has rank $c+e$. Thus composition is regular with additive codimension. This is the direct definitional argument of Tag 065K.

Let $g:V\to S$ be separated smooth of relative dimension $r$, and $s:S\to V$ a section. The separated-section lemma gives that $s$ is closed. Both $V\to S$ and $S\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}S$ are smooth (the identity has the unique lifting property and is finitely presented), so the smooth-pair lemma supplies regular equations for $s(S)$ locally. To compute their length, use a compatible affine section $R\to B\to R$ with composite the identity and ideal $J=\ker(B\to R)$. Apply the smooth conormal exact-sequence theorem with $A=C=R$ and $I=0$: it gives $J/J^2\cong\Omega_{B/R}\otimes_B R$. Smooth differentials have rank $r$, while conormal freeness says the rank of $J/J^2$ is the length of the regular equations. Hence that length is $r$. The argument is local along the section, so affine restrictions suffice. It also applies when $r=0$.

proof.text: On compatible affine charts of a smooth morphism over a regular scheme, the ring map is smooth and the base ring is regular. The smooth-ascent theorem says precisely that its target ring is regular. Thus these charts give regularity of the smooth source scheme. In particular affine space over a regular scheme is regular, because its projection is smooth of the specified relative dimension.

source.place: Tag 07NF, lemma-regular-goes-up; morphisms.tex smooth affine charts and affine-space smoothness

proof.text: Write $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $Y=\operatorname{Spec}B$ for the given finite-type affine morphism. The all-affine-pairs characterization of local finite type shows that $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-algebra. Choose generators $b_1,\ldots,b_n$. By the definition of finite-type algebra the evaluation homomorphism $A[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\twoheadrightarrow B$, $t_i\mapsto b_i$, is surjective. Its spectrum is a closed immersion $Y\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^n_X$. Affine space is regular by Step 6, so Steps 1 and 2 prove that this immersion is regular. The same argument proves regularity for every closed immersion of $Y$ into an affine space over $X$, since both schemes in the immersion are regular.

source.place: morphisms.tex Tag 01T2, lemma-locally-finite-type-characterize; Tag 00NR applied as in Steps 1 and 2

proof.text: For a smooth morphism $p:P\to X$ of relative dimension $r$ between Noetherian schemes, fix $z\in P$ and $x=p(z)$. Smoothness implies flatness, local finite presentation, and smooth fibres by the smoothness criterion; by the definition of a flat morphism the local homomorphism $\mathcal O_{X,x}\to\mathcal O_{P,z}$ is flat, and both local rings are Noetherian. Apply the flat height formula to this local map with $\mathfrak Q=\mathfrak m_z$, so that $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak m_x$: $\dim\mathcal O_{P,z}=\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}+\dim(\mathcal O_{P,z}/\mathfrak m_x\mathcal O_{P,z})$. The fibre-stalk quotient theorem identifies the last ring with $\mathcal O_{P_x,z}$. On a finite-type affine neighbourhood of $z$ in the fibre, the field dimension formula gives $r=\dim\mathcal O_{P_x,z}+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(x)}\kappa(z)$; here $\dim_z(P_x)=r$ is exactly the relative-dimension hypothesis. Thus $\dim\mathcal O_{P,z}+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(x)}\kappa(z)=\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}+r$. Only the flat dimension equality is used, so no dominance or catenarity assumption is implicit.

source.place: Tag 00ON, lemma-dimension-base-fibre-equals-total; morphisms.tex Tag 02FX and Tags 01VF, 01VB

proof.text: Now let $f=pi$ be a factorization in the statement, put $z=i(y)$ and $x=f(y)$, and work on components with fixed $r,c$. On an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $P$ around $z$ the ideal of $i$ is generated by a regular sequence $f_1,\ldots,f_c$; all $f_j$ lie in the prime of $z$, so by the weak-regular-sequence localization lemma their images form a regular sequence in $\mathcal O_{P,z}$, and the closed-immersion stalk map identifies $\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ with $\mathcal O_{P,z}/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)$. The regular-sequence dimension-drop theorem gives $\dim\mathcal O_{Y,y}+c=\dim\mathcal O_{P,z}$. The Noetherian-local finite-dimension theorem ensures these local dimensions are finite, so the extended dimension equality is an equality of ordinary integers. A quotient local-ring map induces an isomorphism $\kappa(z)\cong\kappa(y)$. Substituting into Step 8 and rearranging yields exactly $r-c=\dim\mathcal O_{Y,y}-\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(x)}\kappa(y)$. The right hand side only uses $f$ and $y$, proving independence. By local constancy of smooth relative dimension, and Step 2 for $c$, the difference is locally constant on $Y$.

source.place: Regular-sequence dimension drop; morphisms.tex Tag 02G1; intrinsic virtual dimension as in ILO XVI Definitions 2.5.1–2.5.3

proof.text: For completeness, the finite-fibre formulation of quasi-finiteness in the statement agrees here with isolated fibre points. For a finite-type morphism with finite fibres, every affine open of a fibre is the spectrum of a finite-type field algebra with finite spectrum. The finite-spectrum theorem says all its primes are maximal. Thus all points of the fibre are closed; as there are finitely many, each singleton is open (its complement is a finite union of closed points). Each fibre point is therefore isolated. Apply the isolated-fibre-point residue theorem to conclude that $\kappa(y)/\kappa(x)$ is finite. A finite field extension is algebraic: the powers of any element are linearly dependent over the base. Thus no singleton is algebraically independent, so its transcendence degree is zero. The formula of Step 9 specializes as claimed.

All local statements above are asserted at points of the immersed or smooth source. If that source is empty there are no points to check. The empty tuple is regular in every nonzero local ring, has ideal zero and conormal rank zero, so the arguments include codimension zero. In the section case $r=0$ gives conormal rank zero and an empty local defining tuple. In the dimension calculations $r=0$ or $c=0$ is ordinary substitution in the same equalities.
